title: Choosing the Appropriate Architecture Style
subtitle: Choose the least-worst fit for this domain and its constraints
summary: Pip has several plausible architectures for the growing bookshop. The choice depends on domain shape, data, organizational readiness, and qualities that need separate scopes. Communication follows those constraints; examples show trade-offs rather than one universal winner.

concepts.title: Why Styles Shift
concepts.body: Pip hears that every modern shop should use the same new platform. Styles shift with earlier pain, tools, new capabilities, ecosystem change, and external pressures such as mergers or licensing. A trend matters when it changes practical forces. Pip checks skills, elasticity needs, and migration cost before replacing a stable system.

concepts.title: Decision Inputs
concepts.body: Pip invites data experts and operators before choosing a style. Domain, structural qualities, existing data, organizational constraints, process, and team knowledge all shape feasibility. A design requiring mature automation can fail where that practice is absent. Pip includes legacy integration and strategic needs rather than evaluating topology alone.

concepts.title: Isomorphism and Quanta
concepts.body: Pip’s customizable product resembles a plug-in core, while many parallel processors suggest a different topology. Domain/architecture isomorphism asks whether problem shape fits style shape. Quantum analysis distinguishes one shared quality profile from different profiles needing distributed boundaries. Pip uses both tests to justify topology and its added coordination.

concepts.title: Communication as a Consequence
concepts.body: Pip locates data before deciding how components should communicate. Synchronous calls are convenient to design and debug; asynchronous work can improve scale, elasticity, or isolation with races and coordination costs. A half-second payment provider needs buffering when auctions finish together. Pip queues that constrained workload while keeping a simple short lookup synchronous.

concepts.title: Case Study Trade-offs
concepts.body: Pip compares the book’s two businesses before drawing the shop’s next boundary. Silicon Sandwiches can use a modular monolith or customization microkernel with simple deployment. Going, Going, Gone separates unequal bidder, auctioneer, stream, tracking, and payment needs through services and queues. Pip retains the costs of orchestration, data separation, and network calls alongside each benefit.

misconceptions.claim: The newest or most popular style is automatically the best choice.
misconceptions.correction: Popularity reflects changing conditions and past pain, but the domain, characteristics, data, organization, and team determine fit. A stable monolith can be the least-worst choice.

misconceptions.claim: Asynchronous communication is the modern default for distributed systems.
misconceptions.correction: Asynchrony offers specific scale and performance benefits while adding synchronization and debugging problems. The chapter recommends synchronous communication by default and asynchronous communication when necessary.

scenario.title: Choose a shape for a new service
scenario.context: A small team is building a sandwich ordering product with modest traffic, a limited budget, and a requirement for customer-specific menu rules. A second initiative is an auction platform with bursty bidder traffic, a read-heavy stream, and a payment provider with a fixed processing rate. You must choose a style per context and explain which characteristics drive the boundary.

options.label: Modular monolith
options.benefit: One deployment and one database keep operations and coordination simple for the modest ordering system.
options.cost: Independent scaling and deployment are limited, and customization needs explicit domain design rather than structural plug-ins.
options.consequence: The small team can ship the ordering flow quickly and keep related transactions simple. If demand or team boundaries change, separated tables and components leave a possible migration path.

options.label: Distributed services
options.benefit: Auction functions can scale and evolve with different characteristics, while queues buffer the payment bottleneck.
options.cost: Network calls, data boundaries, deployment automation, and asynchronous failure handling increase operational and design complexity.
options.consequence: Bid capture and streaming can absorb different loads from payment. The team must pay for observability and coordination, and should avoid distributing the simple ordering product merely for fashion.

scenario.debrief: The two contexts produce different least-worst choices. Architecture style follows the forces and domain topology; the same organization may reasonably use a modular monolith in one area and distributed services in another.

quiz.question: Which finding most strongly supports a distributed architecture?
options: Different parts need materially different architecture characteristics
The team has seen a popular distributed style online
The code could be divided into many classes
quiz.explanation: Different characteristics imply separate quanta may be needed. Popularity and class count do not by themselves justify runtime distribution.

quiz.question: A domain consists of highly coupled multipage forms where each page depends on prior context. Which reasoning is best?
options: A highly decoupled distributed style may fit poorly; consider a more coupled style
Microservices is ideal because every page can be its own service
Data architecture can be ignored until after deployment
quiz.explanation: Semantic coupling makes fine distribution difficult. The chapter uses this kind of domain as an example where a less-decoupled style may fit better.

quiz.question: What should justify adding asynchronous messaging between two components?
options: A demonstrated need for scale, performance, or isolation that outweighs added coordination
A desire to make every architecture look distributed
The assumption that asynchronous calls are always faster
quiz.explanation: Asynchronous communication introduces race conditions, synchronization, and debugging costs. It earns its place when a real constraint requires its benefits.

exercise.title: Write a style decision
exercise.prompt: For a system you know, list the domain forces and architecture characteristics before choosing a style. Record whether one quantum is enough, where data lives, and why communication is synchronous or asynchronous.
